evidence: src/presentation/http/LoanController.ts lend(): `const loan = await this.lending.lend(...); await this.history.note(loan.id, 'lent');` puts the rule that a lend must be recorded in history in the presentation layer.

src/presentation/http/LoanController.ts giveBack(): `const fine = await this.lending.giveBack(body.loanId, new Date()); await this.history.note(body.loanId, 'returned');` repeats the same history rule for returns.
renderLoan(loan), the HttpResult status codes (201/200) and the request interfaces are proper presentation responsibilities.
parsedVerdict.reasoning:
Most of LoanController is normal presentation work. It defines the LendRequest and ReturnRequest request shapes, maps request fields to service calls, renders the response through renderLoan, and builds HttpResult status codes.

The problem is that the controller also sets a business workflow rule: every lend and every return must be written to loan history. In both lend() and giveBack() it calls the core operation on LendingService and then calls LoanHistoryService.note(..., 'lent' / 'returned') itself. That rule belongs in the business layer (kind: domain). Because it lives in the HTTP controller, any other way of lending or returning a book would skip the history record. The two writes are also not coordinated: if history.note fails, the loan state has already changed. The orchestration should sit in LendingService or an application service in the business layer. historyOf() is a simple pass-through and is fine.

Confidence is moderate because some designs accept light orchestration across services in a controller.

violations.message: lend() and giveBack() decide that each lend/return must be recorded via LoanHistoryService.note(..., 'lent'/'returned'). This business workflow rule belongs in the business (domain) layer, e.g. inside LendingService, not in the HTTP controller.
